83.s: The studio floor was lightweight concrete on pads, with the drummer on a separate platform and baffles around.
83.q: Concrete was a studio. Right. Yeah, oh, I'm, yeah, I'm sorry, yeah, no, no. Studio was concrete. Right. What, what the studio was, was, uh, there was a, there was a, uh. Extremely live.

83.t: Drum miking, room reflections and the live studio sound
83.s: Matassa moves from one or two drum mics to five to seven, and explains the live room, late reflections and the dead rear.
83.q: Well, by, by, by the time I got there, I was using many more microphones than before. Remember, I used to do mics with, do drums with one or two mics. Mm-hm. And I got to doing five, six, and seven microphones on drum kits.

83.s: Matassa recorded live albums and radio shows with audiences in the studio, which changes absorption and EQ.
83.q: Well, we, we, we did a couple of recordings where they wanted them live. So we, we'd invite in a hundred friends and put them out there in chairs and, to make it a live recording. Like it was in a club or something. And, uh, then I started doing some radio shows. Mm-hm. With audiences. And, and,…

83.t: Changing recording technology: effects and dry tracks
83.s: Matassa lists plates, tape delay and springs, and describes bigger consoles and monitoring EQ while recording dry.
83.q: Yeah. Yeah. And by that point I had two, uh, plates for, for artificial reverb. Mm-hm. I had, uh, tape loop delay. I had, uh, digital delay. Um, I even used a couple of spring reverb, uh, you know, kind of built into the guitar amps. Right. I had a couple of those that I, that I rigged up myself to…

83.t: The big room, ice air conditioning and the three-track machine
83.s: The new big room could hold a string section; he cooled it with crushed ice and fans and got a three-track tape machine, while the union barred overdubs.
83.q: it's something scraping the tape is what it is the for the first time other than when I did remote jobs on location somewhere there was room enough for instance to set up a string section at the same time and and and and because we were catching hell about we wanted to do overdubs the union…

83.t: Mono, two-track mono, and Sea Cruise
83.s: Everything on Rampart was mono; two-track mono let a voice be put over another band track, as Frankie Ford did on Huey Smith's Sea Cruise; stereo came late.
83.q: no everything was everything was mono everything was mono yeah even when I got to having just before I left I wound up with a two track machine it was two track mono we were recording like maybe the band on one track and the vocalist on another and that we continued that kind of a practice when we…

83.t: Bouncing and overdubbing on three tracks
83.s: With three tracks he could bounce and overdub rhythm, horns and vocals, often recording the band in stereo and adding to it, though he resisted it, preferring live playing.
83.q: okay which meant that you could say record basic rhythm a piano drums and bass or maybe and guitar rhythm guitar on one track and then play that track and add percussion more guitars whatever maybe some extra drum or whatever combine the live thing coming from the studio with what was off the tape…

83.t: Resisting multitrack; four-track only at Camp Street
83.s: Many records still sounded live, vocals could be punched in, and he did not get four-track until Camp Street around 1965 when others had eight to twelve tracks.
83.q: by that time everybody else was up to 8 and 12 right there were a few machines made 12 track one of the one of the tape machine companies made a 12 track machine still on one inch tape instead of eight and a lot of people used that and then then to 16 and 24 now I'm 32 and up

83.t: Eight-track mixer and miking more instruments
83.s: Moving from a four to an eight-channel mixer let Matassa mic instruments independently instead of balancing by placement; large groups were hard.
83.q: It allowed me, number one, to mic more things independently and get a little bit better balance that wasn't physical by placement of the people in the room, because that was always difficult. And if you had more than five players, it was really difficult. Did you often have more than five? Oh,…

83.t: Bunny Robyn, the West Coast mastering engineer
83.s: Master Recorders engineer Bunny Robyn mastered for Imperial and the independents and improved Matassa's poorer recordings.
83.q: You didn't do it. I couldn't... You couldn't do it. Now, I'll say this. There was a guy, Bunny Robine, who was the mastering engineer for Imperial and all of the independents just about on the West Coast at master recorders. Bunny Robine... And that's spelled O-R-O-P-Y-N incidentally. Uh, uh, uh,…

83.t: Control room design and monitor speakers
83.s: The control room layout, the argument over live versus dead rooms, and Matassa's Tannoy and Altec monitors.
83.q: It, it was at the front of the building. Right. Right. Which meant it separated the studio from that street noise. Yeah. Okay. It, it, the floor was raised. Right. It had a ramp up at the back end. Yeah. Okay. Right. And then you had the raised floor. And at the front was a recessed area right at…

83.t: Line-level EQ on vocals and no mixing in mono
83.s: He bought a separate mic preamp for the vocalist to use the line-level EQ; with direct-to-mono recording there was no mixing afterwards.
83.q: There was no... There was no...

83.s: Explains EQ for presence and brightness, boosting lows, and filters versus equalizers; the first board at J&M had no EQ at all.
83.q: One is in the mid to upper range to increase or decrease presence or brightness. In the low mid range you increase presence. 2,500K, 2K, 3K, 1,000 Hertz. Right. Okay. Okay. In the upper, you know, from 5, 7, up like that, the brightness. Okay. So if you could increase that, you would increase it…

83.t: From two-track to three-track tape, film origins, and Les Paul
83.s: He explains the move to half-inch three-track tape, its film origins, early eight-track users Atlantic and Les Paul, and Les Paul's guitars and multitrack and speed effects.
83.q: okay and the reason for the half inch tape was to give you wide enough tracks to have a decent signal to noise ratio the tape tape business was still evolving

994.t: Click tracks across changing time signatures
994.s: He explains doubling the click to a common denominator, and that 'We Came Through the Storm' was cut without a click.
994.q: Yeah because it depends on what it is. Because if there’s a lot of time signature changes you can find the common denominator and you can change the click track to the common denominator –

426.t: Studio design for producers and removable control room windows
426.s: The control room was designed so the producer sits apart from the engineer, and windows can be removed for players.
426.q: That’s different from anybody else. All of the other agents work in somebody else’s facility, either at home or some kind of for hire place. Everything I’ve done is relevant to this room, Hackensack and here.
